drills.q: Explain the structural difference between an NSG and an ASG, and why Azure split them into two objects.
drills.a: NSG is the actual filter (prioritized allow/deny rules on IP/port/protocol, attached to subnet and/or NIC). ASG is a group label assigned to NICs that an NSG rule references instead of a hardcoded IP. Decoupling means rules stay valid as VM IPs churn during scale-out or redeployment, since ASG membership -- not current IP -- is what matters.

drills.q: A team's NSG rule creation fails with an opaque error during a large migration. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The NSG likely hit its hard 2,000-rule ceiling (custom + default combined) -- a migration wave creating many narrow IP-specific rules approaches this fast. Fix: consolidate via augmented security rules (multiple IP ranges/ports in one rule) or move to ASG-based grouping. The limit cannot be raised.

drills.q: Explain why Application Gateway and Front Door are not interchangeable, and describe a production topology combining both.
drills.a: Application Gateway is regional and VNet-scoped with no cross-region awareness. Front Door is a global anycast edge service with health-probe-driven cross-region failover. Production pattern: Front Door Premium at the global edge (WAF, CDN, failover) in front of per-region Application Gateway v2 instances handling VNet-internal path routing and private backend connectivity.

drills.q: A team creates a Private Endpoint but clients still reach the PaaS resource's public endpoint. Diagnose.
drills.a: The Private DNS Zone (e.g., privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) was never linked to the VNet, so clients still resolve the resource's public FQDN to its public IP instead of the private endpoint's IP. The private endpoint exists but is effectively unused until DNS is wired correctly.

drills.q: Does creating a Private Endpoint for a Key Vault automatically prevent public internet access to it? Explain the security review implication.
drills.a: No -- public network access is a separate resource-level setting. A Private Endpoint adds a private path without removing the public one unless the resource's public access is explicitly disabled, which should only happen after confirming every legitimate client has migrated to the private path.

drills.q: Compare VNet peering's transitivity to a Transit Gateway-based AWS hub-and-spoke design.
drills.a: VNet peering is explicitly non-transitive: A peered with hub B, and B peered with C, does not let A reach C without an explicit A-C peering or an actual router (Azure Firewall, NVA, or Virtual Network Manager mesh). AWS Transit Gateway functions as a router providing transitive routing between attached VPCs by design -- Azure's closer analog for that behavior is Virtual WAN, not plain VNet peering.

drills.q: A hub VNet approaches its peering connection limit as spoke VNets are added. What's the fix and what's the limit?
drills.a: Default VNet peering supports up to 500 connections per VNet. Fix: adopt Azure Virtual Network Manager's connectivity configuration, which raises the ceiling to 1,000 peered VNets and centralizes peering/security-rule management across the estate.

drills.q: Explain Application Gateway v2's pricing model and why it can surprise a team used to AWS ALB.
drills.a: Fixed gateway-hour rate (~$0.443/hour) that accrues regardless of traffic, plus variable capacity-unit consumption (~$0.0144/capacity-unit-hour) scaling with load. An idle/low-traffic gateway still carries a meaningful fixed cost floor -- provisioning one gateway per small service across many services accumulates surprising fixed cost versus consolidating behind one shared gateway with path-based routing.

drills.q: Design network segmentation for a three-tier app (web, app, data) using NSGs and ASGs.
drills.a: Create three ASGs (asg-web, asg-app, asg-data), assign each tier's NICs accordingly. NSG rules: allow asg-web -> asg-app on the app port, allow asg-app -> asg-data on the DB port, no rule allowing asg-web -> asg-data directly. As instances scale or churn, ASG membership keeps segmentation correct with zero rule changes.

drills.q: Why would a Front Door Premium deployment enable a backend origin with zero public IP, and what feature makes this possible?
drills.a: Front Door Premium supports Private Link origins, letting the global edge reach a regional backend via a Private Endpoint even with no public network exposure at all -- closing the old requirement that anything behind Front Door needed some public reachability. This is Premium-only; Standard tier does not support Private Link origins.

drills.q: Compare Azure's regional VNet model to GCP's global VPC model and state the concrete multi-region design implication.
drills.a: A GCP VPC spans all regions globally with per-region subnets under one object, so multi-region connectivity needs no peering at all. Azure VNets (like AWS VPCs) are regional -- multi-region connectivity requires explicit Global VNet Peering or a hub service like Azure Virtual WAN, an entirely additional connectivity layer a GCP-native design wouldn't need.
